speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very prosaic statement after all this by-play. As I announced in the house on May 19, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation offered mortgages to approved lenders and investment dealers at auction in the form of 30 parcels, each covering different geographical areas and each valued at approximately $500,000. The tenders on this issue closed on Monday June 19, at 11 a.m., and I should like to announce to the house the results of this first sale of mortgages at auction.
The mortgages offered all carried an interest rate of 6J per cent with approximately 25 years to run. The average accepted tender across the board was at a premium, at 101.17, and in this connection I might explain that the bidders for these mortgages are all professional buyers of securities who know it costs about one point to put an investment of this kind on their books. Hon. members will therefore understand that, when this cost is deducted from the bid price, the tenders are at about par.
Of the 30 parcels offered for sale, there were five on which no bids were received. On the remaining 25 parcels, worth approximately $12J million, the total bids amounted to $31 million. Allotments of the $124 million have already been made to the successful bidders. In this first auction bids were received from chartered banks, life insurance and trust companies and investment dealers, a fairly representative cross section of those who can be expected to develop a secondary market in mortgages.
The results of the auction are such as to encourage a second offering to the growing mortgage market. In order that dealers may have time to dispose of the first issue, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation undertook not to make a second offering before the 18th of August, and it is likely that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will make its second offering about that time.

1.	Was Mr. Mieczyslaw Wilk a landed immigrant?
2.	If so, on what date was he landed?
3.	Did Mr. Wilk apply for the admission to Canada of the wife he had married by proxy?
4.	If so, was his wife within the category of persons admissible under the existing immigration regulations?
5.	If not, for what reason?
6.	Is Mrs. Wilk a prohibited person under the Immigration Act?
7.	Was the application for her admission refused for other than merely technical reasons?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer is as follows:
1.	Yes.
2.	January 5, 1959.
3.	Yes.

4,	5, 6 and 7. Section 20(c) of the immigration regulations provides for the inclusion, within the categories of persons admissible to Canada, of the wife or fiancee-including the proxy wife-of a person who is a citizen by birth or naturalization of any country of Europe and who has been legally admitted to Canada for permanent residence.
Mr. Wilk's application for his proxy wife, therefore, came within the general provisions of this regulation. However, because of the limited examination facilities available to the department in respect of applications on behalf of residents in Poland, it is not possible to deal with all applications falling within the admissible categories set out in regulation 20(c). In accordance with policies established in 1956 and still in effect, the actual processing of applications is therefore generally limited to applications submitted by Canadian citizens.
Since Mr. Wilk, at the time of application, had not been in Canada long enough to acquire Canadian citizenship, he was advised that it was not possible to proceed further with his application at the present time; but that, if he wished to renew it at a later date, it would then be given further consideration.
Since, for the foregoing reasons, Mr. Wilk's application could not be proceeded with, medical and other aspects of Mrs. Wilk's examination for admission to Canada were not completed. It is not therefore possible to state whether or not Mrs. Wilk is a prohibited person within the meaning of the Immigration Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monteiih (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: SUPPLEMENTARY ASSISTANCE TO OLD AGE PENSIONERS, B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer is as follows.
1.	The federal government has always been prepared to share, under section 8 of the unemployment assistance agreement, in additional relief payments to recipients of old age security pensions as well as to recipients of old age assistance, blind persons allowances and disabled persons allowances. To be shareable, such payments have to be made on the basis of an individual assessment of need which takes the requirements as well as the income of an applicant into consideration. British Columbia began making payments on this basis, effective September 1960, and these are being shared by the federal government.
2.	(a) The answer I have already given covers this point.
(b)	The unemployment assistance agreement under which the payments are being made authorizes the federal government to reimburse the province to the extent of 50 per cent of its assistance payments.
(c)	The province has been gradually transferring recipients from its supplementary allowance program under which eligibility was based on a means test, to its supplementary social allowance program which is based on a needs test. This progressive transfer is reflected in an increase in shareable amounts in the claims submitted each month. Provincial supplementary social allowance payments to old age security recipients included in reimbursement claims were $92,041 in September, $119,975 in October and $147,561 in November, the last month for which complete figures are available. The number of persons assisted in each of these months was 5,557; 7,170 and 8,774 respectively. It is anticipated that the number of persons covered by this program will increase for some months because of the continuing transfer of persons from supplementary allowances. If the above figures for old age security recipients are added to the figures for recipients of the three above mentioned assistance programs, the total federal and provincial payments for the months of September, October and November 1960 are

This amendment would become important only if by proclamation pursuant to section 87 imports and exports of oil were made subject to licence. The amendment itself removes from section 20 the present requirement that the board would have to hold a public hearing in every case involving the

National Energy Board Act issue, cancellation or suspension oi a licence for the importation or exportation of oil.
Oil, unlike gas, is not generally traded on a long term basis, and in the event that it did become necessary to licence the import or export of oil, the licence would be for a maximum period of one year and would probably be for a term of six months. There would undoubtedly be a large number of applications, and it would be virtually impossible for the board to hold a public hearing in each case.
The board informs me that it would be its intention to hold public hearings from time to time to give the industry an opportunity to make representations in regard to any regulation or formula which might be adopted to determine the method of computing the amount of crude oil or products which an applicant for an import or export licence would be entitled to. I also remind the committee that the governor in council would have to approve any licence to import or export crude oil or products.

I recognize that the practice would be, in the event of the import of oil, for licences to be granted only for a short term, although there is nothing in the act that I can see which prevents the national energy board, if it so desires, granting a licence for a very long term. There is no statutory protection on that point. However, I think it is reasonable that within the industry such licences, if granted, would be for a short term. Since they are for a short term, the method of public hearings is not feasible and would appear in many instances to be unreasonable in relation to the problem confronting the board with respect to possible oil import licences.
However, there are two problems that concern me. This amendment is made necessary by the reference to section 87 of the act, and would only become of real significance in the event that the governor in council took action under section 87 to bring the import of oil under the provisions of the act.
That raises, of course, the old point that was a point of real difference at the time the act itself was before the House of Commons. I refer to the argument that the governor in council should never have been given the power to take that arbitrary action. The authority to bring the import of oil under control in a nation that has wide trade interests, as this nation has, and a nation that is so dependent on trade, as this nation is, is a right which should never have been granted to the government without some need being demonstrated for the government to have that power. The need has not been demonstrated.

The amendment of this section, bearing in mind that the amendment can only have significance if the government has taken action under section 87 to bring the import of oil under control, raises in my mind at once the question, has the government in mind bringing the import of oil under control? Section 41 requires the filing of certain technical information respecting international power lines, and section 43 prohibits operation of an international power line without first obtaining a certificate. speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce

I should like to explain this clause. By deleting the words "from any place within a province to any place outside the province", the application of the section is extended to the intraprovincial transmission of gas by a company to which the act


applies, where the gas transmitted through its pipe line is the property of the company. This has the effect of enabling the national energy board to fix tolls for the transmission of all gas through a pipe line subject to federal jurisdiction where such gas is owned by the pipe line company, regardless of the origin or destination of the gas.
I think the house will appreciate the fact that once gas is injected in a pipe line it becomes indistinguishable as to origin or destination. We have one pipe line company which at the present time picks up gas in Alberta and British Columbia and delivers gas at points in British Columbia for consumption in that province, and exports the balance of the gas at the international boundary. As the section stands now it would be impossible for the board to segregate the gas produced and sold in British Columbia and fix tolls on the balance. There is also the implication that some other authority would have the right to fix tolls on the gas produced and sold in British Columbia, or alternatively that no tolls could be fixed for the transportation of gas produced and sold in British Columbia. This is an impossible situation.
By deleting the words "such proportion as the board may fix" of the differential between the amount paid for the gas and the amount for which the gas is sold, recognition is given to the impracticability of devising any general formula for the equitable determination of the portion of the difference that is to be deemed a toll. The amendment would have the effect of permitting the board to rely upon the differential between the cost to the company of the gas and the amount for which the gas is sold as the toll in the case of a company that owns the gas being transmitted. The use of this differential is considered appropriate in this case inasmuch as recognized public utility practice requires that gas transmission companies calculate their earnings as a return on the amount of investment in useful facilities employed in providing the transmission service. There is no profit permitted on the actual purchase and sale of the gas. The costs associated with the purchasing and selling of gas are expenses.
The amendment would also substitute for the phrase "the amount paid by the company for the gas" the phrase "the costs to the company of the gas", to make it clear that any amount charged to the company for bringing the gas to the point where it enters the company's pipe line, for example an amount charged by a provineially incorporated gathering system, shall be a part of the cost to the company of the gas and, therefore, excluded from the amount of the deemed toll, subject to the jurisdiction of the board.

357. Remedial works where damages are caused by, or endanger, navigation or federal government structures, $800,000.

I wonder whether the minister is going to reply to the remarks that were made by the hon. member for Hull on the question of remedial works and whether discussion should take place between the federal government and the provincial governments with regard to the responsibility for such remedial works.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I would be very happy to do so. On previous occasions, both verbally and by correspondence, I have tried to enlighten the hon. member for Hull on this matter. Because of the mood of the house today I will go no further than to say that I have tried to do so. Apparently I have failed and so I shall make one more effort. Incidentally, I am not referring to the hon. member for Levis.

The history of this matter is that back in the thirties there was an unemployment relief vote whereby funds were provided to carry out work which was not necessarily a federal responsibility. This included protection works. Subsequently, when the vote was discontinued, a general vote respecting protection works was instituted, but by 1954 there were so many demands on this vote that it would have cost the government hundreds of millions of dollars to meet these requests which were not a federal responsibility.
In 1954 the wording of the vote was changed. It was changed, incidentally, by the administration in which the hon. member for Levis was the distinguished parliamentary assistant to the then minister of public works. The hon. member will recall that the vote was changed to provide funds for work which the federal government should carry out.
There are two principles involved. The first is that the British North America Act places property and civil rights under the jurisdiction of the provinces, and the shoreline of every lake, river and creek comes under the property category. It includes water lots, and it may be of interest to point out that in the construction of our various wharves and other projects we are obliged to obtain from the province the administration and control of the shore line and water lot property for the life of the project. There can be no argument, in so far as erosion is concerned, as to the shore lines of our many waters in Canada not being a provincial responsibility. As a matter of fact, there seems to be no question about that.
The second principle involved relates to navigation and here we have a responsibility. The control of navigation was retained by the federal government at the time of confederation and the law in that connection has not been changed up to the present time. As a result, therefore, we have the Navigable Waters Protection Act which is administered by the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works. The Department of Transport administers that portion dealing with hazards to navigation and is particularly concerned with ship channels. Derelicts or wrecks of ships constitute examples of such hazards.
The Department of Public Works administers that portion of the act relating to the construction of projects under, across or over navigable waters. From this federal responsibility with respect to commercial navigation channels we get a connection between maintaining that channel, which we do through the Navigable Waters Protection Act, and
Supply-Public Works
even by dredging, and the damage that shipping does the nearby shore line.
There is doubt, of course, that erosion caused by shipping is legally a federal responsibility but it has been assumed as such and I think that the responsibility possibly exists. However, erosion from flooding or from natural causes cannot be included in this category and in accordance with the British North America Act that remains the responsibility of lower levels of government.
Shore erosion is also often caused by manmade structures such as docks, wharves and bridges which disturb the natural flow and change the course of the water thus causing erosion. Those responsible for the construction of such projects should be held responsible for the damage thus caused through erosion. The federal government accept this principle and is prepared to repair damage done under these circumstances. This explains why the vote relating to protection works is confined to the expenditure of money for erosion where it is caused by commercial navigation or where there is a federal structure involved. Much as I should like to extend that limit to please different members on both sides of the house, the frightful cost to the federal government in assuming a responsibility that is not a responsibility of the federal government would be so great as to make it a burden which no federal government could possibly bear.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
In reply to the hon. member for Gloucester I would say this bridge was commenced in 1958. At the moment, we call it the Campbellton-Cross Point bridge. It is an interprovincial bridge extending between Campbellton, New Brunswick and Cross Point, Quebec. The department retained the consulting firms of Langevin, Letendre and Monti and Paul Pelletier to prepare the design and supervise the construction of the bridge. The total crossing is 4,180 feet long; the Quebec causeway portion is 960 feet; the New Brunswick causeway portion is 620 feet, and the bridge spans 2,600 feet. There are ten river piers on the main span. Tenders for the substructure were received on November 18, 1958, Ten bids were received, the lowest being that of Belle Construction Limited of He Maligne, Quebec, in the amount of $1,261,592.70. The balance of the bids ranged from this figure up to $1,681,746. Belle Construction Limited, the low tenderer, had not previously done work for this department. However, enquiries of the province of Quebec and private organizations for which they had done work brought favourable reports as to their technical and financial capacities. The contract was awarded to Belle Construction Limited on December 12, 1958.
On March 30, 1960, construction of the substructure was completed, except for minor works. The contractor submitted a claim for payment of $1,343,216.45 over and above his contract amount. In the departmental review of the claim, there were a group of items pertaining to additional work required to be undertaken by the contractor as a result of changes made in the design. These changes were made at our specific request. On these items, the audit services division of the comptroller of the treasury carried out a cost audit of the contractor's books to establish the actual amount assessed against the items approved by the department. This totalled $150,913.61.
The second part of the claim had to do with the fact that the contractor had to carry out the work throughout the winter of 1959-60, whereas he had originally contemplated completing it before the severe portion of the winter season set in. The total amount claimed by the contractor for this portion was

$561,033.64. The audit services division, on examination of the contractor's books, assessed the items claimed as being $453,815.32. In reviewing this claim, the department took the stand that our contract provided for the work to be done and it was the responsibility of the contractor to complete the work before the winter season set in. However, the department did acknowledge that, as a result of certain design changes, the original period for completion of the contract would have to be extended. The extension period was not in itself, however, sufficient to require the contractor to work throughout the winter season and he had, by his own operations, to a large degree created the condition requiring this winter work. On the basis of this, the department felt it should share in these costs proportionately to the additional time resulting from the changes in design. On this basis, it recommended payment of $170,180. The total amount recommended by the department was $321,094.36 against the claim of $1,343,216.45. This recommendation was passed by the treasury board.
The contractor was, as might be expected, dissatisfied with the amounts recommended by the department and placed the matter in the hands of his solicitors who advised they would not accept. The department re-examined its proposal at great length and on many occasions but did not feel that any change should be made. On the advice of the Department of Justice, the department advised the solicitors that the department's offer was firm and, if not accepted, the contractor could take court action. The contractor has now accepted the department's decision and payment on the basis outlined above is being made.
So, to sum it all up, the original contract price, without any changes by us, was $1,261,592.70 which was the lowest of ten bids, the highest being $1,681,000. The changes that we caused were assessed at $150,913.61 for the first part, as well as increased quantities at $34,924.94, and for the second part $170,180 so that the total settlement for the bridge is $1,617,612.00 The amount claimed was $1,343,216.45 and this claim was settled at $321,094.36. The hon. member for Gloucester asked whether this sum had all been paid. No, it has not. There is still a hold-back.

I should like to say a few words on this item with respect to the trans-Canada highway because of its construction through national parks. I do so at the request of a number of persons in my constituency. Since in certain circumstances the trans-Canada highway is not an all-winter road, the suggestion is that consideration be given

to making a second trans-Canada route along the southern provincial highway of British Columbia. The southern provincial highway will provide service through a better type of terrain for maintenance purposes. There is less snowfall. It would serve directly a much larger local population and provide several roads for access to United States roads. In this connection I wish to mention an editorial which appeared in the Trail Daily Times of January 16, which deals with the question of the trans-Canada highway being closed because of slides and things of that sort and yet at the same time there was transportation through the southern provincial highway. In one paragraph this editorial writer says:
What are the lessons here?
Well, if Mr. Gaglardi and other members of the provincial cabinet are C.B.C.-T.V. fans, they must have learned several from their television screens on Saturday.
That afternoon, the C.B.C. carried a feature about long-distance road users operating between Vancouver and Calgary and beyond. Asked why his trucks invariably travelled from Vancouver through Everett, the Snoqualmie pass, Wenatchee, Spokane, and back into Canada through Kingsgate, the proprietor of the haulage firm was quite specific:
"The mileage Is greater, it is true.
But we are able to make much better time in spite of the greater distance.
The trans-Canada highway isn't opened in the winter all the way from Vancouver to Alberta.
Anyway, the American highways are so much better."
His comments on the state of the trans-Canada to one side, the trucker made no reference whatsoever to highway No. 3, and the C.B.C. interviewer didn't ask him about the southern trans-provincial either.
Probably neither of them liked to think about the Rossland to Cascade section just before lunch.
That is being changed this year.
But the first lesson came when the C.B.C. showed the long distance truck stopping every two hours in the United States so that its crew could eat, and then taking on 150 gallons of fuel in Spokane.
I know this is not an immediate question but I have been asked to raise it because in British Columbia we believe that when the trans-Canada highway is completed-I am not suggesting that we should undertake more than two things at once-consideration should be given to making the southern trans-provincial route a second route as part of the trans-Canada highway.
There is another matter I wish to raise in connection with the new highway bridge over the Columbia river just west of Revel-stoke. On my way to the house I was taken there by an engineer. I was informed that the bridge is nearly completed and will have cost close to $3 million. I was shown the elevations placed on the bridge by engineers which indicate that if the high Arrow dam is built the water will come within three or four feet

of the deck. There will be no opportunity for large chunks of ice to pass under the bridge and when the level of the water behind the dam is at its peak, which will be for several months during the high water period, there will be no opportunity for logs and forest debris to pass under the bridge and no opportunity for navigation whatsoever on what have been navigable waters for many years.
I was asked to bring this matter to the attention of the minister. As a matter of fact, I had a question on the order paper which was passed as an order for return. I should like to ask the minister whether consideration has been given to this problem in the event of the building of the high Arrow dam. The engineer who took me to the site said that it was not possible to raise the bridge because it is a suspension bridge. I know nothing about that. He also referred to the C.P.R. bridge and the present highway bridge, all of which would have to be renewed. Incidentally, I have a photograph taken from the air by a friend of mine who is interested in the project and chartered a small plane in order to do so. I should like the minister to inform the committee whether this problem has been given consideration and, if it is correct that the about to be completed trans-Canada highway bridge, to which the federal government has made a contribution of 50 per cent, I presume, will be unusable should the high Arrow dam be built, what will have to be done to correct the situation.

Mr. Chairman, I must exhibit some disagreement with my confrere from Kootenay West and I hope that his persuasive voice and gentle manner will not influence the minister too much in the matter of a second trans-Canada highway. We always look upon the southern part of British Columbia, as other provinces perhaps look upon their southern portions close to the border, as getting the gravy with respect to all public services while those of us in the north limp along on what is left over.
On a number of occasions I have raised the question of the development of a second trans-Canada highway and in general terms have suggested the route that should be followed. I wish the minister would pay a great deal of attention to the area between Prince Rupert, Prince George and Jasper as being the route that should be followed in the building of a second trans-Canada highway. While the hon. member for Kootenay West may be somewhat upset about this, I am sure such a route will be much more acceptable and beneficial to the population in the northern part of the province than would an additional so-called trans-Canada highway in the southern part.
All jocularity aside, this is a very serious matter and one of prime concern to the people living in the northern part of British Columbia as I am sure it also is to those living in the northern parts of other provinces. As far as east-west travel is concerned, we are somewhat restricted because of a lack of roads. The minister knows our provincial minister of highways fairly well, I believe, as he is in touch with him regularly and he must be aware that that gentleman constantly gloats about the amount of money being spent on highways in our province each year and every day in the year. The fact still remains, however, that highway 16 in the northern part of British Columbia is not a decent highway. The fact still remains that there is no direct road connection east and west between Prince George and Jasper in Alberta, and it would appear to be a sensible approach to develop a highway through this part of the province under an arrangement similar to that existing now with respect to the trans-Canada highway.
I disagree with the member for Kootenay West, the Prime Minister and others who say that we should complete the present trans-Canada highway before we start another one. In this regard I would make a brief reference, as I did earlier, to the report of proceedings under the Trans-Canada Highway Act for the fiscal year ended March

Supply-Public Works 31, 1960. The report indicates that Saskatchewan has fully completed its section of the trans-Canada highway. The province of Alberta has only four miles of paving to complete before finishing its section. Manitoba has but eight miles remaining to be finished and, as I said earlier, British Columbia has some 152 miles to complete. I do not know whether the Hillsborough bridge in Prince Edward Island has been completed but in any event Prince Edward Island is another province which has nearly completed the building of its section of the highway.
I point out that in the three prairie provinces there are only 12 miles of the trans-Canada highway remaining to be completed while in British Columbia there are some 152 miles. Other provinces have greater mileages to complete, relatively speaking, compared with the mileages they had to build initially. So far as the four western provinces are concerned, when we start to think in terms of a trans-Canada highway, I think we can take steps to start on that second trans-Canada highway right now without waiting for the first trans-Canada highway to be completed from one end of the country to the other. This completion date gets moved ahead every two or three years and is now the end of December, 1963, I believe. In all probability, if past experience is any guide, this 1963 date will be extended when we get close to that period of time. This will mean that some parts of Canada, for a variety of reasons, will find that they will have to limp along continually or limp along until such period of time as the first trans-Canada highway is completed and will have to work on their own with their own finances in developing in the northern part of the province a system of roads which may later on become part of a second trans-Canada highway after the first one is completed. This may require relocation. It may require roads at present being built to fall into disuse by reason of another route being chosen and it could easily result in an extra expenditure of money both from the provincial treasury and the federal treasury if we wait until the last mile of the present trans-Canada highway is completed, and until we can drive from one end of the country to the other.
So far as I am concerned and so far as the people of my constituency are concerned and, I am sure the people in the constituencies in that general northern part of the four western provinces of Canada, a start can and should be made on the development of a second trans-Canada highway tomorrow or as soon as possible or as soon as arrangements can be worked out with the various provincial governments. I think that all that would be necessary, to start it at least, would


be an approach made to the provincial governments by the Department of Public Works or the federal government saying that they are interested and want to work out an arrangement somewhat similar to that which exists with regard to the present trans-Canada highway.
I think this will not be looked upon with too much favour by those individuals, organizations and groups, especially those in my own constituency with whom I am familiar, who have campaigned, pressed, petitioned and written letters about the start of a second trans-Canada highway and who now have it underlined that they will have to wait until the last province completes the last mile of the highway before we will even think about starting on a second one.
I should like to make a comment or two, if I may, about the formula for financing the building of such highways. At the present time it is on a 50-50 basis plus an additional 40 per cent of 10 per cent of the mileage in a province. As I have mentioned on other occasions, such a formula which moves on the assumption that conditions are equal as between each province and every part of Canada and therefore the financial participation should be equal is an incorrect one, in my opinion. For instance, I think that a new formula, once developed, should take into account the difference in construction costs between various parts of the country. I think everyone will know, for argument's sake, that in British Columbia which is a very mountainous region, with a great deal of rock work, some tunnels to build, bridges and the like, construction costs in many cases run in the neighbourhood of $1 million a mile. This is a rather fantastic amount of money to be considering when you are concerned with three or four hundred miles of road through mountainous country of that nature.
I am quite sure that, by comparison, the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba do not have road building costs that are nearly as great as are those experienced in British Columbia. Yet the formula implies or has implicit in it the feeling that road building costs are equal. I believe that some move should be made to adjust the formula now, just as it was adjusted on one occasion earlier, to take into account different road building costs and geographic factors so that those provinces which have high road building costs will not thereby be penalized, as it were, in the building and construction of the trans-Canada highway and of the second trans-Canada highway.
I also think that in the formula itself some consideration should be given to reflecting the

relative financial positions of the various provinces and their ability to find money at the provincial level with which to finance the building of highways. Let us consider Newfoundland, for instance. I pick this province because it is at one end of the country and British Columbia is at the other end. Each has substantially the same number of miles to build on the present trans-Canada highway, Newfoundland having 554 miles and British Columbia 568 miles.
So far as the financial position of Newfoundland is concerned compared with that of British Columbia-and this is not said in a derogatory way; I think it is a fact and that members from Newfoundland have mentioned this matter on other occasions, and I am sure they will agree with me now-it is extremely difficult for Newfoundland, because of its economic conditions and financial position, to finance the building of highways in that province to the same extent as, say, the province of Ontario, a rich industrial province or the province of Alberta or British Columbia. I think this fact must be reflected in that formula also.
We take into account the differences in economic conditions of the maritime provinces, for argument's sake. We take that into account in other matters by special grants. Reference was made to those grants last evening by the Minister of Finance in the introduction of what he has called the budget and for which I have other names. However, the budget took into account the fact that there is a different economic situation existing in the Atlantic provinces and that therefore some special financial consideration should be given to those provinces in the way of grants. I do not see why we do not have that same attitude or feeling reflected when it comes to participating financially with provinces in the building of highways. I think the formula should be adjusted accordingly so that a higher ratio of money will go to those provinces which are in a less fortunate economic position and will thereby have a tendency to balance out the differences financially between the various provinces.
There may also be other factors that it would be necessary to consider and to have reflected in such a formula. I think those two factors of road building costs and the ability to pay are the most important ones. One may deal with the question of mileage, for argument's sake, or the relative mileage as between Prince Edward Island with 71 miles and Ontario with some 1,400 miles, I believe or 1,453 miles and say that perhaps this factor also should be reflected in the amount of money that is contributed by the federal government.

These are matters which I am sure could be worked out on a formula basis after the economics have been studied. I am sure a mutually satisfactory agreement could be reached with the various provinces in regard to such a formula that would reflect the factors I have mentioned, such as the rocky country compared with the prairies, the relative economic position of a province like Nova Scotia compared with Ontario, and so on, in order that equitability is reached throughout.
I only mention these matters-I have mentioned them before-because I hope they will be given consideration. I understand from what the minister has said that he agrees with the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Kootenay West that a start should not be made on the second trans-Canada highway until the first one is completed. I disagree with this entirely and so do all the people I represent.
The minister holds the view, in agreement with the Prime Minister that no move should be made toward building a second trans-Canada highway until the first one is completed, and I know this pretty well ties the hands of the minister in making any definite reply with respect to the approach to the provinces with respect to the formula and the like. However, if the minister would like to hold out some hope-and I know that members of the government have great propensities in this direction-of a change of attitude with respect to this construction policy of not starting on the second highway until the first one has been completed, at least it will be helpful to hon. members of the committee and to the people I represent. Perhaps this ray of hope will be enough to make them a bit more patient than they are likely to be if the policy of not starting on the second one until the first one is completed is carried through to the time when the last shovelful of asphalt is put in place and the last ribbon is severed.
I appreciate that the Department of Public Works is only partially involved in this question by virtue of the machinery of the department for building the trans-Canada highway being also involved in some way with building the so-called roads to resources. I think in these matters, also, a straight 50-50 participation is not-

A vast new area is being opened up there. A road up the

coast of Labrador as well as through the interior is highly desirable and would serve the purpose of opening up new territory. Eventually, when the second trans-Canada highway is built, a road through Labrador, perhaps through a tunnel under the straits of Belle Isle and then down the coast of the northern peninsula of Newfoundland, might be kept in mind by the government as a great new project worthy of consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to refer to a matter of general public importance relating to municipal road closings in the province of Ontario. I suggest this subject falls within the discussion of the minister's estimates because there is a land registry within the Department of Public Works in connection with land requirements.
Briefly I should like to state that road closing by-laws in the province of Ontario require the approval of the governor in council if federal government land is involved. For many years applications for approval which have been made under this by-law have been approved only after the receipt of a letter from the Department of Transport stating that it had no interest in the area involved. Until this time the provincial government authorities have been satisfied to accept such a letter from the department. Last fall, in September I believe, a decision was reached by the administrative section of the Ontario municipal affairs department as a result of which a general certificate from the federal government stating that no crown lands are involved is required. This change is of concern to me because, by reason of this ruling, which I think is ridiculous on the part of the provincial government department, the approval in respect to approximately 15 road closings for subdivision development plans in the district of Muskoka is being held up. I suggest there are perhaps many other such delays experienced by other communities in the province of Ontario.
I understand the land registrar and the Clerk of the Privy Council have been attempting to organize federal departments so that such certificates could be provided. It is my understanding that the land registry of the Department of Public Works is not prepared to circularize the other departments so that their files could be searched in a speculative manner. This is the only way that certificates could be issued as to whether crown lands are involved.

Mr. Chairman, first of all, I wish to thank the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) for the new grant of over a million dollars he has kindly made to the Jeanne Mance housing development in the constituency of St. James. This grant will greatly help the city of Montreal to complete that project which I would say is of prime importance from a social point of view. As a matter of fact, the Jeanne Mance housing development has had remarkable success. All apartments are now occupied and while opposition members offered some criticism, there is now a long list of applications for that development. In fact, hundreds and even thousands of applicants are on the waiting list.
I also want to congratulate all those who contributed to the success of the project, namely the personnel of C.M.H.C., the staff of the Jeanne Mance housing development, and particularly the present manager, Mr. Leopold Roger.
Mr. Chairman, that waiting list of applicants for homes in the Jeanne Mance project shows the urgency of implementing the studies on urban redevelopment made by the city of Montreal, thanks to federal subsidies. In fact, two of those studies have now been completed, one concerning slum clearance and the construction of low rental housing in the eastern part of the city, the other concerning the general slum conditions throughout the city.
I know that the reports on those studies have been produced, and it is urgent, indeed, to implement them, especially with respect to the slum clearance project which is required for the C.B.C. project in Montreal east. The implementation of those reports is urgent, because there is some concern, at present, as a result of the delay and procrastination involved in the carrying out of that project.

Mr. Chairman, I also want to congratulate the Minister of Public Works who recently invited municipalities to take better advantage of the National Housing Act for studies involving slum clearance and town planning.
Town development across the country fully justifies the invitation extended by the minister urging municipalities to make use of such financial assistance as C.M.H.C. can provide for effective town planning projects.
Mr. Chairman, I want to point out to the minister that federal assistance to urban redevelopment is too strictly limited to housing. In my opinion, such subsidies should be provided within a larger frame so as to help municipalities in general town planning, the emphasis being on housing.
Cities are becoming more and more important in Canada. It has been proved that, in a period of one year, two cities the size of Ottawa are being created in this country and it seems that the tendency toward more and larger cities will be on the increase as years go by. I am sure we should take into consideration the attitude adopted in the United States toward urban development. You have an example there. They have reached a point where President Kennedy is considering having a municipal representative in his cabinet.
Mr. Chairman, one must remember-and I speak here as a representative from a city riding-that a Department of Agriculture was created some generations ago because agriculture was of vital concern at that time. It has probably remained so, although there is no doubt that urban development and the difficulties encountered by the cities in their expansion plans have taken a national importance. For those reasons, it is surely desirable to enlarge the scope of the National Housing Act so as to promote town planning, redevelopment of the older cities, and the development of new cities all across Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to call the minister's attention to another point, which concerns co-operative housing.
It seems that under the National Housing Act assistance has been provided for people whose yearly income is less than $3,500. That would cover subsidized housing, such as the Jeanne Mance project.
There is also the financial assistance which, thanks to direct guaranteed loans of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, is given to those whose salary is over $5,000. Therefore, there is a sort of no man's land between those who earn less than $3,500 and

those who earn more than $5,000, where the National Housing Act does not provide any practical assistance.
As a matter of fact, I recently had the opportunity of studying a co-operative housing project in the north of Montreal, where this difficulty was encountered, in spite of substantial help from authorities of the city of Montreal. There was under the National Housing Act, no means of helping people with an income between $3,500 and $5,000 to enjoy low rental housing, and such an income represents the salary of the great majority of people in the larger cities like Montreal. In the United States, the housing legislation provides that whoever participates in a co-operative development may deduct from his income tax a certain part of the capital and interest he is paying for his house, or his accommodation. I believe this provision should be examined and similar legislation enacted in Canada, so that co-operatives might overcome this impediment in our National Housing Act.
We would then be able to help our citizens whose income is over $3,500 and under $5,000.

In that case, I completely fail to appreciate how the managers of investment funds of Canada failed to submit a bid on any of the five packages to which the minister referred on motions this afternoon. As I understand it-and I hope the minister will immediately interrupt me if I am wrong -these mortgages carry an interest rate of 6J per cent and are insured as to repayment of principal and interest. Yet not a single

bid was received. Here was an offering to the investment houses of Canada of $12i million worth of paper that had an insured interest rate of 6f per cent. Not only was the interest insured but the basic principal also was insured. However, earlier today the minister informed the House of Commons that not a single bid had been received.
To me this is a horrible indictment of the managers of investment capital available in our nation today. I read the report of the governor of the Bank of Canada as released as recently as Monday last. In it he refers to the resources and the lending capacity of Canadian banks. In addition to the resources available to and the liquidity of the banks of Canada today there are the insurance companies, trust companies, mortgage companies and many other like organizations. We in our group have often called upon the government to assume responsibility for the direction of investment capital. Under the Income Tax Act Canadian corporations, by way of depreciation, depletion allowances and the like, have been able to have at their command hundreds of millions if not in fact billions of dollars for re-investment purposes in the past. Yet if you look at the economic forecasts and the investment picture of the future, you find they are holding back; they are sitting tight. Our banks, insurance companies, trust companies, mortgage companies-our Canadian corporations-are sitting back.
I do not know whether they lack confidence in the administration of our country or whether they are anticipating the day when they can invest their money and get even more than 6J per cent. However, I think they ought to be thoroughly condemned for refusing to submit a single bid on insured mortgage paper offered by C.M.H.C. which is, in my opinion, as completely valid as is the dollar in your pocket or as is a Canadian savings bond. It is a mortgage insured as to repayment of basic principal and interest at 61 per cent. Yet the minister is obliged to report the sad fact this afternoon that not a single bid was received on this offering of five of the 30 packages that he offered.
I congratulated him, as he will recall, on the successful sale of the 25 packages. However, he was obliged to report to the house, not a single bid had been received on the offer of five of the 30 packages. In other words, there was offered $12J million worth of paper insured both as to basic principal repayment and as to return of the interest of 6f per cent and not a single offer had been received.

Mr. Chairman, there is one aspect of housing in which I have a particular interest. I should like to make a brief

Business of the House
comment on it. I refer to housing in so far as Indian people are concerned.
The National Housing Act was amended in 1956 to provide that the corporation may make loans to Indians as defined in the Indian Act for the purposes of housing projects on reserves. I have been given to understand that not one single loan has been made. The reason for that is that not one single application has been made for such a loan.
This matter of home building is of extreme importance to native Indian people. I do not know whether this failure to apply for loans arises because they are not generally familiar with the fact that an Indian can apply to the corporation for a loan, or from the fact that Indian lands are not mortgageable for any purpose whatsoever; they are lands held in trust.
I am inclined to think that the latter reason is the correct one, that is, it is impossible to make loans to an Indian person for home building purposes because he cannot mortgage his land as security for the loan. There are a couple of means which might be used to overcome this difficulty and which I think the corporation should consider, or the governor in council should consider because the amendment to the act says these loans are subject to and in accordance with regulations of the governor general.
Perhaps some way may be found to overcome this particular difficulty and assist Indians to have the same opportunities as non-Indians in so far as borrowing money for home building purposes is concerned. Mr. Chairman, before I get into that question I wonder whether I may call it six o'clock.
